strengths: Addresses a practically relevant problem: localizing cameras using compact floorplans without appearance-specific maps. The combination of pretrained depth features and uncertainty-aware matching is well motivated.

Reports substantial improvements across synthetic and real-world benchmarks. On Gibson, 15-frame success increases from 41.8% for F3Loc fusion to 65.3%; on LaMAR HGE, 100-frame success increases from 36.4% for F3Loc mono to 100%.
Provides useful component ablations. Uncertainty modeling improves sequential localization across all five tested encoders on LaMAR, supporting its contribution beyond simply replacing the backbone.
Includes single-frame and sequential evaluations, reproduced baselines, ground-truth-depth references, runtime measurements, and supplementary grid-resolution and observation-frequency experiments.
weaknesses: The claim of eliminating per-environment training is substantially stronger than the evidence. Section 6.1 explicitly trains models for 50 epochs on each dataset's training split using ground-truth floorplan depths. Reusing a pretrained encoder avoids training a backbone from scratch, but does not eliminate supervised adaptation of the floorplan predictor. The manuscript should distinguish these claims and specify which encoder parameters are frozen.

Evidence for generalization to unseen real buildings is very limited. The HGE-to-CAB experiment contains only two 100-frame sequences, with 50% success at 1 m. Supplementary results show 0% success for 15- and 35-frame sequences without adaptation and only 2.5% single-frame recall at 1 m. These results do not establish robust deployment without target-environment training.

Technical novelty is incremental: the approach retains F3Loc's attention-based depth representation and histogram filtering, adds a standard heteroscedastic Laplace likelihood, and substitutes pretrained depth features. The empirical improvements are meaningful, but the manuscript does not sufficiently position its uncertainty formulation against established probabilistic depth estimation and sensor models.

The strongest real-world claims compare only against F3Loc mono; F3Loc fusion is absent from LaMAR without a clear explanation. HGE evaluation uses just three held-out sessions and 11 long sequences, with no repeated-training variability or confidence intervals. The headline 16.7-fold improvement reflects an increase from 1.2% to 20%, leaving substantial absolute failure rates.

Important technical and reproducibility details are missing or incorrect. Equation 3 omits the previous posterior and sums over the current rather than previous state, so it is not a valid recursive Bayesian update as written. The source and accuracy of evaluation ego-motion, motion-noise parameters, uncertainty positivity constraints, and several discretization settings are insufficiently specified. The filtering equation may be a presentation error, but it requires correction.

Uncertainty evaluation establishes downstream utility but not calibration. There are no coverage or calibration measurements, and the ablation changes both training and inference, leaving their individual contributions unresolved. Efficiency claims also require qualification: the large model takes approximately 1.065 seconds per frame on HGE, and fewer required frames do not by themselves establish lower wall-clock time to localization.

strengths: Addresses a practical localization problem using compact floorplans, with substantial reported improvements across synthetic and real-world datasets.

Sequential results are convincing within the evaluated settings: Gibson success at 15 frames increases from 41.8% for F3Loc fusion to 65.3%, while full-HGE success at 100 frames increases from 36.4% for F3Loc mono to 100%.

Useful controlled ablations separate pretrained encoder improvements from uncertainty modeling. Uncertainty improves sequential performance across multiple encoder architectures, supporting its practical value.
Includes single-frame evaluation, runtime comparisons, smaller-model experiments, and supplementary analyses of grid resolution and observation frequency.
weaknesses: The claimed elimination of per-dataset training is not supported by the main experiments. Section 6.1.1 explicitly trains models on each dataset for 50 epochs, using supervised floorplan-depth targets. Reusing a pretrained encoder does not eliminate training of the custom prediction module; the abstract and contribution statements substantially overstate this distinction.

Evidence for generalization is very limited. HGE training and testing use different sessions from the same building, while the cross-building CAB experiment contains only two 100-frame test sequences. Without adaptation, CAB success is 50% at 1 m, and shorter-sequence performance is poor even at 2 m. These results do not establish broad deployment without environment-specific training.

Technical novelty is incremental: the method combines pretrained depth features, standard heteroscedastic Laplace regression, and the existing F3Loc attention/filtering framework. The paper does not sufficiently position its uncertainty formulation against established uncertainty-aware regression and probabilistic localization methods.

The strongest real-world claims compare only against F3Loc mono; F3Loc fusion is evaluated on Gibson but omitted on LaMAR without a convincing explanation. HGE's headline 100-frame result uses only 11 sequences from three test sessions, and no confidence intervals or repeated-run variability are reported.

Equation 3 is not a correct recursive Bayesian filtering update as written: it omits the previous posterior and sums over the current state rather than the previous state. This may be a presentation error given the reliance on F3Loc, but the implemented recurrence needs clarification. Reproduction is also hindered by unspecified motion-input provenance, filter noise parameters, encoder freezing policy, and uncertainty positivity constraints.

Uncertainty is evaluated through downstream accuracy and qualitative examples, without calibration or coverage measurements. The independent-ray likelihood assumption and the sensitivity to the constant scale used in the no-uncertainty baseline are not examined.

Efficiency claims need qualification. The main model takes approximately 1.07 seconds per HGE frame on a workstation GPU, and its Gibson feature extraction is roughly an order of magnitude slower than F3Loc mono. Smaller-model results are encouraging, but fewer required frames do not by themselves establish lower wall-clock time to localization.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem: visual localization using compact floorplans. Integrating predicted depth uncertainty into map matching is well motivated, particularly for ambiguous or occluded indoor observations.
The sequential localization improvements are substantial. On Gibson at T=15, success rises from 41.8% for F3Loc fusion to 65.3%; on LaMAR HGE at T=100, it rises from 36.4% for F3Loc mono to 100%.

Ablations provide useful evidence for both components. On HGE at T=35, adding uncertainty to the same depth backbone increases success from 42.9% to 60.0%. Similar improvements across multiple encoders strengthen the empirical case.

Evaluation includes synthetic and real imagery, multiple sequence lengths, single-frame localization, runtime measurements, and supplementary grid-resolution experiments. The small-backbone results also demonstrate a promising accuracy–runtime tradeoff.
weaknesses: The claim of eliminating per-environment training is substantially stronger than the evidence. Section 6.1.1 states that models are trained for 50 epochs on each dataset's training split, using ground-truth floorplan depths. Using a pretrained encoder does not eliminate training the floorplan prediction network. The manuscript should distinguish backbone pretraining, supervised head training, and deployment without target-domain adaptation.

Evidence for generalization to unseen buildings is weak. The CAB experiment contains only two T=100 test sequences, with 50% success at 1 m. Supplementary results show 20% success at T=50 and zero success at T=35 and T=15 without adaptation, even using a 2 m threshold. This does not establish broadly reliable out-of-environment deployment.

The methodological novelty is limited: UnLoc largely retains F3Loc's architecture and histogram filtering, substitutes a stronger pretrained encoder, and adds standard heteroscedastic Laplace regression. The ablations establish usefulness, but comparisons against tuned constant uncertainty, robust matching alternatives, or uncertainty added to the original F3Loc backbone would better establish the distinctive contribution.

The probabilistic formulation needs correction and validation. Equation (3) omits the previous posterior and sums over the current state rather than the previous state; as written, it is not the claimed Bayesian filtering recursion. This may be a presentation error, but it affects the central method description. Moreover, no calibration or coverage analysis establishes the quality of the predicted uncertainties.

Important evaluation and reproduction details remain unclear, including the source and accuracy of relative motion and gravity inputs, which encoder parameters are frozen or fine-tuned, and key filter settings. HGE's longest-sequence result uses only 11 sequences from three test sessions, without uncertainty estimates or repeated-run variability. The strongest F3Loc fusion baseline is also absent from the main real-world comparison.

Efficiency claims need qualification. The large model takes about 0.178 seconds per frame on Gibson versus 0.018 seconds for F3Loc mono, and approximately 1.065 seconds per frame on HGE. Fewer frames to convergence do not automatically imply shorter wall-clock localization time. The smaller-model and coarser-grid experiments are useful, but the broad real-time claim is not established.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant localization problem with a coherent integration of pretrained depth features, learned uncertainty, histogram filtering, and trajectory refinement.

Reports substantial improvements on Gibson and LaMAR HGE. Importantly, the matched-encoder comparison demonstrates benefits beyond upgrading the backbone: at T=35 on HGE, uncertainty increases success from 42.9% to 60.0% before post-processing.
Provides useful ablations across encoder architectures and sizes, uncertainty distributions, grid resolutions, and observation frequencies, alongside single-frame and sequential evaluations.
The HGE-to-CAB transfer experiment provides some evidence of cross-building generalization, and the appendix transparently describes manual floorplan preparation and alignment.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is incremental: heteroscedastic Laplace regression and uncertainty-weighted residuals are established techniques, while much of the architecture and filtering pipeline follows F3Loc. The empirical evidence must therefore carry much of the contribution.

The claims of eliminating environment-specific training are overstated. Appendix A.1.1 explicitly trains models on each dataset's training split for 50 epochs, and the pretrained encoder feeds a supervised floorplan-depth head. Cross-building evidence is limited to one transfer pair, with only two T=100 test sequences and 16.7% success at T=15. A matched-backbone transfer baseline is missing.

The largest short-sequence gains are not adequately isolated from retrospective trajectory reconstruction and refinement. On HGE at T=15, post-processing raises success from 20.0% to 50.6%. This procedure reconstructs the evaluated last ten poses from the final posterior before optimizing them; equivalent reconstruction and unweighted refinement are not reported for the baselines. Consequently, the headline improvement does not isolate uncertainty modeling or demonstrate equivalent gains in online convergence.

The probabilistic specification has a substantive presentation error: Eq. 3 omits the previous posterior and sums over the current state rather than the previous state. It therefore does not express the described Bayesian filter. Uncertainty calibration is also unevaluated, and the independence assumption across correlated image columns is not examined.

Important reproducibility and deployment details remain unspecified, including the source and accuracy of ego-motion, whether the encoder is frozen, how positive uncertainty scales are enforced, and how gradients are obtained through occupancy-map raycasting during refinement. There is no sensitivity evaluation for motion errors, despite reliance on ego-motion in both filtering and backward trajectory reconstruction.

Statistical and practical claims exceed the evidence. HGE long-sequence results use only 11 sequences, CAB uses two, and no repeated-run variability or confidence intervals are supplied. The default HGE extraction and matching require about 1.065 seconds per frame, plus 0.96 seconds for final refinement, qualifying the real-time claim. These limitations, together with the comparison gaps, place the paper slightly below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant problem: sequential camera localization using compact floorplans. Combining uncertainty-aware depth matching with trajectory refinement is a useful extension of F3Loc.

Reports substantial improvements on both Gibson and LaMAR HGE. On 15-frame Gibson sequences, UnLoc achieves 81.3% success versus 41.8% for F3Loc fusion; on HGE, it achieves 50.6% versus 1.2% for F3Loc mono.

The evaluation includes meaningful controls beyond the original baseline. Backbone-matched comparisons and experiments across five encoders consistently support a benefit from uncertainty modeling in sequential localization. Additional experiments examine Gaussian versus Laplace likelihoods, grid resolution, and observation frequency.
weaknesses: The contribution is primarily incremental: pretrained depth features, standard heteroscedastic Laplace regression, F3Loc-style histogram filtering, and weighted trajectory optimization. The empirical improvements are promising, but the paper provides limited methodological novelty beyond this combination.

The claim of eliminating environment-specific training is overstated. The method trains a custom floorplan-depth and uncertainty predictor, and Appendix A.1.1 explicitly trains models on each dataset's training split for 50 epochs. Using a pretrained encoder does not make the complete predictor an off-the-shelf, training-free module. The manuscript should clearly distinguish source-domain training from deployment without target-domain adaptation.

The largest gains are not fully attributed. On HGE at 15 frames, replacing the backbone improves success from 1.2% to 9.4%, uncertainty raises it to 20.0%, and post-processing raises it to 50.6%. There is no corresponding backbone-matched baseline with uniform-weight trajectory refinement, or uncertainty-trained model evaluated with constant matching weights. These controls are needed to isolate the value of predicted uncertainty from refinement and changes in depth training.

Evidence for generalization is limited. HGE training and testing use different sessions within the same building. The cross-building CAB evaluation contains only two 100-frame sequences and 18 15-frame sequences, with 50% and 16.7% success respectively at 1 m. It also omits the important F3Loc-plus-Depth-Anything baseline. No repeated-run variability or confidence intervals are reported.

Important technical details remain unresolved. Equation 3 omits the previous posterior and sums over the wrong state variable, so it is not a valid recursive Bayesian update as written. This may be a presentation error, but it requires correction. The paper also does not explain how gradients are obtained through occupancy-grid raycasting for post-processing, how positive uncertainty scales are enforced, or whether the pretrained encoder is frozen.

Uncertainty quality and deployment robustness are insufficiently validated. There are no calibration or coverage measurements, and the source and accuracy of evaluation ego-motion are unclear. The manually aligned floorplan ground truth has no quantified independent alignment error. Finally, the broad real-time claim needs qualification: the main HGE configuration takes approximately 1.07 seconds per frame, plus 0.96 seconds for final refinement, on a desktop GPU.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant localization problem and integrates uncertainty-aware depth matching, pretrained depth features, and trajectory refinement into a coherent pipeline.

Controlled comparisons demonstrate benefits beyond simply replacing the encoder. On LaMAR HGE, uncertainty modeling increases 35-frame success from 42.9% to 60.0% without post-processing; on Gibson, it increases 15-frame success from 56.3% to 65.3%.

The complete system achieves substantial improvements on short sequences: 81.3% success on Gibson and 50.6% on LaMAR HGE at 15 frames. Comparisons with F3Loc using the same depth encoder are particularly informative.

The ablations cover multiple encoders, model sizes, uncertainty distributions, grid resolutions, and observation frequencies. Reporting sequence counts, unsuccessful-run errors, and runtime improves transparency.
weaknesses: The claim of eliminating environment-specific training is overstated. Section A.1.1 explicitly trains models on each dataset's training split for 50 epochs, and the method learns a custom floorplan-depth and uncertainty head. Pretrained encoder reuse does not establish deployment without environment-specific training. The only unseen-building experiment is small: CAB has just two 100-frame test sequences, with 50% success at 1 m.

Post-processing substantially confounds the headline comparison. It reconstructs the last ten poses backward from the final estimate and refines precisely the window used for evaluation. This is legitimate retrospective estimation, but does not directly establish earlier online convergence. Baselines need equivalent backward reconstruction and refinement, including an unweighted refinement ablation. On HGE at 15 frames, post-processing alone raises success from 20.0% to 50.6%.

The algorithmic novelty is limited: heteroscedastic Laplace regression, pretrained depth encoders, histogram filtering, and weighted geometric refinement are established components. The application-specific integration is useful, but its significance depends heavily on rigorous attribution of the empirical gains.

Important technical and reproducibility details are missing or incorrect. Equation 3 omits the previous posterior and sums over the current rather than previous state; this is not a valid recursive Bayesian update as written. The source and accuracy of ego-motion inputs, encoder freezing policy, and differentiation through occupancy-grid raycasting during refinement are insufficiently specified.

Real-world validation is concentrated in one training building and one small transfer experiment, without repeated-run variability or confidence intervals. Manually modified floorplans and affine alignment from four manually identified correspondences introduce unquantified ground-truth uncertainty. Broader transfer tests and sensitivity to odometry and map errors are needed to substantiate robustness and scalability.

Uncertainty quality is assessed mainly through downstream success, without calibration or coverage measurements. Likewise, the real-time claim needs qualification: the main HGE configuration takes about 1.07 seconds per frame on a workstation GPU, plus approximately 0.96 seconds for final refinement.
